 Election Day in America
 • Polls open: Voters in several US states are casting their ballots , joining millions who did so before Election Day. Early voting data, from before today, offered a glimpse into who turned out compared with previous cycles. The first polls are due to close at 6 p.m ET.
 • High stakes: Democrats, who need to win three seats to capture the House and four seats to win the Senate, enter Election Day with a 9-point advantage in the generic congressional ballot, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls . The GOP’s redistricting strategy will be put to the test and the party is defending Senate seats in firmly red states.
 • On the ground: The Justice Department says around 1,000 election monitors have been deployed to all 50 states. Voting issues have been reported in the key swing district of Westchester, New York, and flooding in Florida forced 19 polling locations to move.
 • Stay with us: Follow CNN’s tracker of when to expect results and sign up for breaking news email alerts to get key updates.

 21 Florida polling places moved due to weather emergency
 By Andy Rose 
 A person drops a vote-by-mail ballot in a secure ballot intake station at the Office of the Supervisor of Elections during early voting in the 2026 midterm elections, on October 27, in Doral, Florida. 
 Lynne Sladky/AP/File 
 Dangerous flooding across central Florida is forcing election officials to scramble for alternative polling locations.
 As of 9:30 a.m. ET, the secretary of state’s office said 21 locations had been moved in Brevard, Broward, Highlands, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach and St. Lucie counties. In many cases, precincts are being merged into open poll locations.
 “For the safety and security of our election workers and the voters of Brevard, it is necessary to relocate a couple of precinct polling locations due to these unprecedented circumstances,” Brevard County Supervisor of Elections Tim Bobanic said in a statement.
 The changes, which were announced with less than 24 hours notice, are permitted under state law “in cases of emergency and when time does not permit compliance” with the usual notice requirements.
 Gov. Ron DeSantis declared an emergency on Monday covering seven counties, citing “a significant threat to the safety, security, and well-being of Floridians in portions of Florida.”
 This post has been updated with additional information.

 A snapshot of one of the most vulnerable GOP seats in Congress, a few miles outside NYC
 By Katherine Koretski 
 One of the most vulnerable Republican seats in Congress sits just a few miles north of New York City, in a district former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024.
 Incumbent Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, who has held the seat since 2022, is in a tight race against Biden administration alum and combat veteran, Democrat Cait Conley. This seat could play a crucial role in Democrats’ attempt to flip control of Congress.
 New York’s 17th district includes counties like Westchester, which has historically leaned Democrat, as well as counties like Rockland and Putnam that have recently leaned more in favor of the GOP.
 Lawler, who flaunts his crossover appeal with his voting record in Congress and willingness to break with President Donald Trump, has also leaned into marketing himself as a family man from Rockland County, living with the same struggles as its voters. He secured several endorsements from across the aisle this election cycle, including from Maine Rep. Jared Golden and local Democratic politicians.
 Conley, who served as Director for Counterterrorism on the National Security Council under President Biden, has highlighted her years of service as an Army combat veteran and her desire to lower costs for residents across the district. Conley struggled with name recognition in the early stages of the race.
 This race has been one of the most expensive in this year’s election cycle, with millions flooding in from both sides of the political aisle. Over $40 million was spent cumulatively on ads tying Lawler to Trump and scrutinizing Conley’s connection to AI companies.
 It was also a hot spot for prominent politicians from across the country to stop. Conley was joined on the trail by Democrats like House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, former Secretary Pete Buttigieg and Sen. Mark Kelly. Lawler hosted Republicans like Speaker of the House Mike Johnson and joined Trump at his rally in Rockland County earlier this year.
 The cost of living was a top concern for voters in NY17 when CNN spoke to residents. Many expressed concern about high gas prices, expensive grocery bills, and the rising housing market across the counties.

 Trump's closing message to voters: America is 'hot now'
 By Kit Maher 
 President Donald Trump’s final message to the voter on Election Day is that under his leadership, America is a “hot” country that other leaders now respect, despite a low approval rating among Americans.
 “Well, we have to keep America great. We’re great now,” Trump told Fox & Friends Tuesday morning. “We were terrible two years ago. We were laughing stock all over the world. The leaders of other countries didn’t even take us seriously. They they thought we were fools. And we’re hot now.”
 “You saw oil came down $10 – a record yesterday. Dropped $10, and the Hormuz Strait, we have total control of it with the Navy blockade. I mean, everything’s going good. Everybody respects us again,” Trump said. He also spoke about policies in the One Big Beautiful Bill, like “no tax on tips.”
 Trump said Chinese President Xi Jinping told him during a visit in September: “What you’ve done is amazing.”
 Americans aren’t exactly sharing that sentiment.
 Trump is facing an average 34% approval rating, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls and a record low approval rating of 32% in an October CNN poll. In the same poll, 73% of participants disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy.
 And while Trump celebrated a drop in oil prices, gas prices are at a record high for an Election Day at $4.15 per gallon of regular and $6.29 for diesel statewide, according to AAA .
 On Fox, Trump also touched on a hot button issue: Data centers, arguing that payouts will quell opposition to them being built in American communities.
 “Pay the people. Let them be happy. Give them $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 each,” he said.

 Voting machines unable to scan paper ballots in Westchester County, NY but voting continues
 By Kaanita Iyer 
 Issues with how ballots can be cast throughout Westchester County, New York, stem from voting machines not being able to accept paper ballots, the county Board of Elections said this morning.
 But the county’s nearly 700,000 voters can also cast ballots by hand, officials said. Moreover, the county is looking to use secondary machines that will accept the ballots, said Raquel Brown, executive assistant for Tajian M. Nelson, the county’s Elections Commissioner.
 “The Westchester County Board of Elections (BOE) is aware of an issue involving paper ballots that is preventing voting machines from accepting ballots at polling locations throughout the County,” the elections board said in a statement.
 Elections officials earlier today had pointed to “an issue involving the thickness of paper ballots” before issuing a corrected statement removing the word “thickness.”
 Voters in the county just north of New York City are being asked to fill out ballots that will be placed in secure “orange emergency ballot bags, which will remain secure and monitored” before they are counted, the board said.
 “We strongly encourage all voters to remain in line, exercise patience and, most importantly, cast their ballots,” the statement added.
 “The BOE sincerely apologizes to voters and poll workers for the inconvenience this situation has caused, and the BOE recognizes the importance of a smooth and efficient voting process. They are taking every necessary step to address the issue as quickly as possible.”
 “The Westchester Board of Elections wants to reassure every voter that your vote matters, your ballot will be secure and your vote will be counted,” it said.

 Voting begins in more states with control of Congress at stake. Here’s the latest
 By Maureen Chowdhury 
 People cast their vote at a polling place in downtown Manhattan on Election Day on Tuesday in New York City. 
 Andres Kudacki/Getty Images 
 Election Day is here, and voters in several states have begun casting ballots, with more polls having opened in six states at the top of the hour .
 The stakes are high for both parties as Democrats attempt to gain control of both the House and Senate. Democrats entered Election Day with a 9-point advantage in the generic congressional ballot, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls . Meanwhile, Republicans face tests of their redistricting strategy and their grip on Senate seats in solidly red states.
 Reuters, CNN 
 If you’re just joining us, here’s the latest: 
 Polling sites across Westchester County, New York, are experiencing “issues, ” the state attorney general has said. Attorney General Letitia James assured voters that they can “safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations,” and that “your votes will count.” The county contains part of New York’s competitive 17th Congressional District.
 Recent storms will affect voting today in one of the unlikeliest places: the high desert of Utah . A severe flooding emergency was declared for San Juan County. Residents who can’t make it to a polling place or ballot drop box today may vote electronically, the state has declared.
 The Justice Department this morning shared a list of 126 jurisdictions across the country to which federal election monitors have been deployed.
 Gas prices remains top of mind for voters . A gallon of gas cost $4.15, on average, nationwide on Tuesday, according to AAA. Though the price has been declining in recent weeks, it’s still a record for Election Day.
 CNN’s Catherine Nicholls, Tami Luhby, Kaanita Iyer, Gloria Pazmino, Andy Rose, Mary Gilbert and Holmes Lybrand contributed to this report.

 These states have open races for governor

 People wait in line to vote at Little 5 Points Community Center on Tuesday, in Atlanta, Georgia.

 This includes nine open Democratic governorships and 10 Republican due to term limits of retirements.
 Here’s a look at the state of place across the country:

 In Iowa, anti-trans rhetoric is on voters' minds
 By Betsy Klein in Des Moines, Iowa
 Protesters rally against a bill removing gender identity protections in Des Moines, Iowa, on February 27. 
 Charlie Neibergall/AP/File 
 In the closing stretch of the key Iowa Senate race, transgender rights have become a central part of the political conversation and prompted significant divisions.
 Josh Turek, a Democratic state senator running to replace retiring Sen. Joni Ernst, has been pummeled with ads attacking his record on transgender issues. In the closing weeks of the campaign, he released an ad emphatically stating that he does not support males competing in female sports and opposes taxpayer funds for sex changes. That prompted criticism from LGBTQ+ rights groups and one Democratic official in the state.
 President Donald Trump has often used anti-transgender rhetoric at his campaign rallies, including Sunday in Dubuque. And it’s all broken through to voters.
 David McDonald, a 59 year-old meat cutter from Des Moines, said he decided to split his ticket and vote for Turek’s opponent, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson, because of the ads.
 “I just don’t like the idea of transgender males being able to play girls’ sports,” he said after casting his ballot. “That was a big thing right there for me.”
 Stephanie Campbell, 53, a caregiver from Des Moines who voted for Turek, expressed concern on behalf of the transgender community in her state.
 “Human beings have lost their rights in Iowa, and I don’t even know a single transgender person. But I know just on behalf of the state, it’s not even the same place,” she said.
 For Olivia, a trans woman living in the Des Moines area who asked to have her last name withheld for fear of safety, avoiding television and streaming ads in a campaign cycle has become a survival mechanism. She voted for Turek.
 “At the end of the day, I’m either voting for a party that’s uninformed, or I’m voting for a party that’s actively trying to stigmatize me and remove me and people like me from culture at large,” she said.

 Why Democrats could have a good Election Day
 Analysis by Aaron Blake 
 It’s Election Day, and while there are high expectations for Democrats, it’s impossible to know for certain what will happen in the race for control of Congress.
 Here’s the reasons that could influence why the Democrats have a good result: 
 Trump’s historic unpopularity: By many measures, President Donald Trump is the most unpopular president in modern history heading into a midterm . It’s simply very difficult to win elections — no matter how favorable the Senate map is to Republicans — when people dislike the face of the GOP by a nearly 2-to-1 margin.
 Trump’s coalition broke down: Trump in 2024 made big gains with young people (especially men), Latinos and infrequent voters. But the polls suggest all three groups have turned sharply against him . His tariffs and the Iran war appear to have damaged Trump’s standing with his most reliable and consistent demographic: White voters without college degrees .
 Trump’s neglect of affordability: He was elected in large part because of high inflation under former President Joe Biden and his own promises to fix it quickly. But Trump not only launched policies that exacerbated economic problems , he also called affordability a “hoax” and falsely claimed he had fixed the problem.
 Broken promises: Trump said he wasn’t going to start wars, but he did. He said he was going to fix inflation, and it’s now worse. Podcaster Joe Rogan, who backed Trump in 2024, has been big on this .
 Corruption: There is growing evidence that voters’ concerns about corruption are more of a problem for Republicans than Democrats, perhaps because of a spate of headlines about Trump’s self-enrichment and members of his administration apparently leveraging their positions for financial gain.

 ICE officers go into Election Day like any other, aware of voter concerns if at or near polling sites
 By Priscilla Alvarez 
 Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are heading into Election Day like any other day, though the agency is mindful of the sensitivities surrounding the potential presence of federal immigration agents at or near polling sites.
 In at least one ICE field office this week, leadership reminded officers not to wear agency branding when visiting a polling place to place their votes, according to internal correspondence reviewed by CNN.
 In some previous election years, ICE leadership has also told officers to exercise caution on Election Day and be aware that voters are heading to the polls when conducting enforcement operations, according to three former senior ICE officials.
 Homeland Security officials who spoke with CNN said they had not heard of any changes in operations from department or agency leadership and are not expecting to be deployed to polling sites.
 “It hasn’t even been mentioned as an idea, like ‘we might be doing this.’ Nothing,” an ICE official told CNN, regarding Election Day and ICE being near or at polling sites.
 Asked by reporters in September whether ICE officers could be sent to polling locations, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin left open the possibility that they could be under specific circumstances.
 “The only reason why we would be at polling places, if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. He later added: “If we’re serving a warrant, we will be where we need to be.”
 Federal law generally prohibits “any troops or armed men” being sent to “any place where a general or special election is held.”

 These states could elect their first female governors
 By Jeff Zeleny and Isa Mudannayake 
 Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks in Morrow, Georgia, on October 28. 
 Will Lanzoni/CNN 
 This year’s midterm election is likely to change history as several gubernatorial candidates from the Midwest to the South are vying to become their states’ first female governors.
 Georgia’s Democratic gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms is running to become not only the state’s first female governor, but the first Black female governor in the nation.
 “I wake up as a Black woman every day, so it’s no surprise to me that I’m capable and I’m qualified and I’m able,” Bottoms told CNN. “But if it’s representation for other people who may not have thought that it was possible, then it’s all worth it.”
 Bottoms is locked in a tight race with Republican Rick Jackson in a race that has taken center stage.
 Minnesota is also set to elect its first woman governor, with Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar in a strong position in her race with Republican state House Speaker Lisa Demuth. Tennessee is in the same spot, with Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn leading over Democrat Jerri Green.
 Ohio could also join the list, if Democrat Amy Acton prevails over Republican Vivek Ramaswamy. Although the state briefly had an interim female governor nearly 30 years ago, it has yet to elect a woman to the office.

 How Republicans could have a good Election Day
 Analysis by Aaron Blake 
 It’s Election Day, and while there are high expectations for Democrats, it’s impossible to know for certain what will happen in the battles for control of Congress.
 Here’s the reasons that could lead to a good Election Day for the Republicans: 
 The polls were wrong: A Kansas Senate poll released by The Washington Post last week epitomized the nightmare scenario for Democrats: that polls — especially in red states — could systematically underestimate Republicans because they don’t respond to them as much. It hasn’t been seen as much in the midterms in the Trump era, but that doesn’t mean it couldn’t happen.
 The Senate map was just so red: Even if the margins of the 2024 vote uniformly shifted toward Democrats by 10 points in every state, Democrats would still get to only 49 Senate seats because this year’s battlefield is overwhelmingly made up of Trump states. Democrats need to flip at least two states that President Donald Trump won by double digits.
 The GOP pulled an upset in Maine and/or Michigan: Democrats are defending their seats in Maine, Michigan. They probably should have put those away by now, but haven’t — in part thanks to Democratic Senate nominees who aren’t running as well as the gubernatorial nominees in the same state.
 The GOP’s gerrymandering was too successful: If Republicans keep their majority — or even just keep Democrats’ gains to a minimum — the GOP’s brazen mid-decade gerrymandering push will likely have played a role.
 Voters didn’t care much about top issues: So much of what Trump has done has been unpopular — often by large margins . But if Republicans do better than expected, a big reason might be that voters didn’t care enough about Trump’s actions for them to matter.

 Georgia voters hit the polls early Tuesday morning 
 1:46
 Georgians hit the polls early Tuesday morning to cast their ballots.
 CNN’s Ryan Young spoke to some voters in Dunwoody, Georgia about why it was important to them to get out and vote.
 One woman said she wanted to “send a message to the current administration,” which is that “working people need to have a voice, and that we’re not going to be continuing to give to the 1%.”
 Another man said he wants manufacturing jobs to return from overseas, while another told Young they wanted farmers to be taken care of.
 Watch more in the video above.

 Plot each party’s best path to winning the Senate
 By Byron Manley , Lou Robinson and Matt Stiles 
 As many as 11 key Senate races identified by CNN that are on the ballot in November will likely determine which party controls the chamber.
 Democrats need 51 seats to win majority control of the Senate. Republicans need 50 seats because Vice President JD Vance has the power to cast a tie-breaking vote for the GOP.
 Each party has multiple paths to Senate control. Use this interactive map to see how different hypothetical results would tip the balance. The key races, highlighted in yellow, are those most likely to be in play as polls close on election night. Other races in states with more predictable partisan outcomes are shaded by their current senator’s party.

 Westchester County, New York, polling places facing "issues," NY AG says
 By Kaanita Iyer and Gloria Pazmino 
 Polling sites across Westchester County, New York, are experiencing “issues,” the state’s attorney general has said.
 “My office is monitoring this issue with scanners in Westchester and is in touch with the state and local Boards of Elections as they work on a solution,” Attorney General Letitia James said in a post on X .
 “Westchester voters can still safely fill out and turn in their ballots at their polling locations. Your votes will count.”
 For now, voters in the county just north of New York City are being told to fill out ballots that are then put in emergency orange bags to be counted later in the day, a County Board of Elections spokesperson said.
 “No machines are accepting ballots at this time is what we’ve been told,” said a spokesperson for Rep. Mike Lawler, a vulnerable Republican running in the district that includes Westchester County.
 The issue is “county wide,” the spokesperson said, adding it is not clear if polling locations are having issues with machines or with printing individual ballots.
 “There are technical issues with ballot scanners in Westchester, but don’t worry: you can still vote and every vote is being counted!” said Cait Conley, the Democrat trying to unseat Lawler.
 “The issue is being worked on diligently by the Board of Elections in a bipartisan manner,” Conley said on Facebook . “The Polls are open and operational, and every vote cast will be counted. Please stay in line and have your voice heard as they work to resolve the issue.”
 Lawler also urged voters to stay at polling sites.
 “(E)very very ballot will be counted,” he said in a post on X . “Stay on line and vote. Do not leave the polling place without voting.”

 Polls now open in several states, as election monitors deployed across the US. Catch up
 By Catherine Nicholls 
 Reuters 
 In-person voting should now be open in at least 27 states, with many more polls set to open in the coming hours, until 12 p.m ET.
 A voter carries their ballot at the Brooklyn Museum in New York on Election Day, Tuesday. 
 Yuki Iwamura/AP 
 As Americans get out to vote, here are some of the latest developments:
 Around 1,000 election monitors have been deployed to all 50 states, according to the Justice Department. It shared a list of 126 counties across the country to which federal election monitors have been sent.
 A sweeping emergency order halting many of the aggressive actions the Justice Department has taken towards election officials remains standing after late-night drama at an appeals court.
 As polls prepare to open in the central US, rain is spreading through the region from the same storm that caused historic, deadly flooding in the Southwest over the past few days.
 Meanwhile, 19 Florida polling locations have been moved due to dangerous flooding just 45 minutes before they were supposed to open, the secretary of state’s office said .
 A federal district judge has halted efforts by the Justice and Homeland Security departments to send election officials lists of alleged noncitizen voters.

 Here’s how much the Iran war is costing drivers in your state
 By Tami Luhby 
 The sharp jump in gas prices since the Iran war began in February is weighing heavily on many Americans’ wallets and on many midterm voters’ minds.
 A gallon of gas cost $4.15, on average, nationwide on Tuesday, according to AAA. Though the price has been declining in recent weeks, it’s still a record for Election Day.
 President Donald Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices would fall soon, saying it would happen after the midterm election. But nearly three-quarters of voters disapprove of his handling of gas prices, according to a recent New York Times and Siena University poll .
 Overall, Americans have paid $83.2 billion more for gas since the war began, according to the Climate Solutions Lab at Brown University. That’s about $635 per household.
 But the added burden differs widely by state – with drivers in some places paying a few hundred dollars more and in other places paying over $1,000 more.
 Diesel prices are also at a record high for Election Day at $6.28 per gallon, on average. It’s costing Americans a total of $67.7 billion more to fill up their tanks with diesel, or about $517 per household.
 The extra tab also varies widely by state, with Wyoming and Alaska drivers paying $2,546 and $2,414 more per household. But in Hawaii, drivers are only shelling out an additional $203, according to the Climate Solutions Lab.

 Flooding in rural Utah county prompts state to allow voters to vote electronically
 By Andy Rose and Mary Gilbert 
 Recent storms will affect voting today in one of the unlikeliest places: the high desert of Utah.
 A severe flooding emergency was declared for San Juan County, a picturesque area in the southeastern corner of the state that includes Bears Ears National Monument.
 Residents who can’t make it to a polling place or ballot drop box today may vote electronically, the state has declared.
 “The vast geographic area of San Juan County including rural communities requires traveling extensive distances between residential areas and polling and ballot drop box locations, and flood damage and emergency conditions have made access to the polling places and/or voting drop boxes extremely difficult or impossible,” Lieutenant Governor Deidre Henderson wrote in an emergency declaration on Monday.
 “We do use this method of voting for our overseas and military voters, and for our Americans with Disabilities Act voters,” Henderson, a Republican, told CNN affiliate KSTU . “So, it’s not new. We’ve done this before.”
 Voters with an email address on file with the state will get instructions directly, the declaration states, while those who don’t were pointed to a state phone hotline to request them.
 Between 2 and 4 inches of rain fell in San Juan County over the weekend, according to the National Weather Service, which is triple the amount of rainfall in the area for all of November. The rain has been enough to flood the San Juan River in the southern section of the county near the Four Corners border it shares with Colorado, New Mexico and Arizona.
